meta.title: Who really said "When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it’s Confucius. It’s the closing line of Analects Book 1, Chapter 8 — the exact English is James Legge’s 1861 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Confucius: Analects 1.8, in James Legge’s 1861 translation of ‘過則勿懚改’. Usually quoted without its source.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the closing sentence of the Analects, Book 1, Chapter 8, in James Legge’s 1861 English translation — his rendering of the Chinese “過則勿懚改.” The attribution to Confucius is genuine; the exact English wording is Legge’s.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Analects (論語, Lúnyǔ), Book 1 (“Xue Er” 學而), Chapter 8

source.excerpt: The Master said, ‘If the scholar be not grave, he will not call forth any veneration, and his learning will not be solid. Hold faithfulness and sincerity as first principles. Have no friends not equal to yourself. When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them.’
trail: The line is the closing clause of Analects Book 1, Chapter 8 (Chinese Text Project), which pairs the Chinese 過則勿懚改 with James Legge’s English.
The same wording appears in the MIT Internet Classics Archive text of the Analects: ‘…Have no friends not equal to yourself. When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them.’
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced Confucius section as an Analects line, not among the misattributed quotes.
Legge’s full translation is public domain and available via Project Gutenberg and Wikisource.
source.excerptNote: The familiar line is the final clause of a four-part maxim; it is almost always quoted on its own, stripped of the sentences before it.

source.rightsNote: The Chinese original is ancient and long out of copyright. The exact English wording shown is James Legge’s translation, first published in The Chinese Classics, Vol. 1 (Hong Kong & London, 1861) — well before 1931 — so this specific rendering is also in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: About Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BCE · Chinese philosopher, teacher & political thinker
author.bio: Confucius (Kong Qiu, “Kongzi”) was a philosopher of China’s Spring and Autumn period whose teaching on ethics, family, and good governance shaped East Asian civilisation for two millennia. He wrote no book himself; his sayings survive in the Analects (論語, Lúnyǔ), compiled by his disciples after his death.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely Confucius — the usual problem isn’t who said it but how it’s presented.

items.why: Sites such as Goodreads circulate the line as a free-floating aphorism with no chapter or translator, and often only a vague book title — obscuring that it is the last clause of Analects 1.8.

“When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them” is James Legge’s Victorian rendering of 過則勿懚改; other translators phrase the same line differently, so the exact words are Legge’s, not a fixed ‘original.’

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the attribution are authentic: it is Confucius, from Analects Book 1, Chapter 8, in Legge’s 1861 translation.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The maxim belongs to a compact set of instructions on character: be earnest, keep faithfulness and sincerity central, choose worthy friends, and — the enduring last line — when you find a fault in yourself, don’t cling to it out of fear or pride. Self-correction, for Confucius, is not a weakness to hide but the very engine of moral growth.
